newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian protests plod on amid creeping violence.
newsitem.headline: Serbian protests plod on amid creeping violence.

text.p: Bitter rivals remained deadlocked on Saturday with a solution to Serbia's political crisis nowhere in sight after almost 70 days of peaceful protests over local election fraud.
"There is a rock-solid standoff, the situation is in limbo and the danger of creeping violence is greater than ever," a political source said.
The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, joined by stiudents, has been protesting for 68 consecutive days against election fraud by the ruling Socialist Party (SPS) at November 17 local election.
It claims the SPS stole its victory in 14 Serbian cities, including Belgrade. The claim was upheld by a fact-finding mission by the OSCE last month.
Denying the charge, the SPS, led by President Slobodan Milosevic, claims Zajedno is waging a terror campaign under international tutelage to destabilise the country.
Opponents say Milosevic has remained deaf to Western pressure spearheaded by the United States to restore Zajedno victories, apparently choosing to let the pro-democracy drive exhaust itself.
Milosevic has promised not to use violence against the protesters and on Friday SPS spokesman Ivica Dacic told BBC radio that "force will not be used as long as demonstrations remain peaceful".
But the number of reports of police applying force against the peaceful protesters has increased.
Riot police on Thursday clubbed protesters seated on a highway leading into the central town of Kragujevac, beating one member of parliament unconscious.
Vuk Draskovic, a Zajedno co-leader, told 30,000 supporters at a rally in Belgrade on Friday that another three opposition deputies were beaten and arrested in Cacak, Kraljevo and Krusevac.

As a crowd thronged to the city centre for an unscheduled late-night rally to join students on the sixth day of a round-the-clock stand-off with the police, independent radio stations B92 and Index reported beatings in several districts.
The police was angered at the hide-and-seek game many residents were playing to avoid a ban on marches and forcing the security forces to chase them down dark alleys and parks.
"None of them are Belgrade cops, they have no clue about our neighbourhood. We taunt them, they chase us and we disappear," one boy told Reuters. "It is more exciting that playing cops and robbers."
But the police appeared to have caught on and ambushed one group that came close to the central square, witnesses said.
"Walkers were attacked from the rear by special police who jumped out of darkness, pushed them against cars and beat them. A girl hit on the head was bleeding," Radio Index said.

Despite the sporadic violence, the student protest grew out into a huge open-air disco with tens of thousands of people attending in festive mood denting SPS hopes that the demonstrations will dwindle away.
Associations of actors, artists, librarians, professors, bankers, independent trade unions and singers all joined in.
The librarians offered the police books of poetry but were refused. "Maybe the situation warrants lighter literature," a young woman laughed.
